    With such an array telescope we would get pictures of this and other exoplanets. We might get pictures of that solar system with strange amounts of stuff in front of it that might, might just be a Dyson sphere under construction.

    Doesn't that give you goosebumps? not just pretty pictures but spectrographic data on their atmospheres, their landscapes, maybe see seas, clouds, large continents.

    All this is possible. The ESA is currently flying two satellites in lockstep to demonstrate the tech works before they build a gravity wave detector in space, immune from earthquakes and freight trains and with arms potentially hundreds of km long.

    The keeping your array stable tech from that and the array telescope tech and computation techniques from the radio telescopes mean we can do it with optical range telescope arrays.

    What you're describing is what Alastair Reynolds would refer to as a 'Light Hugger'; a ship capable of reaching around 99% of light speed fairly quickly. The issue with this is that special relativity wouldn't matter in terms of the occupants during departure, as the ship would take so long to reach relativistic speeds that actually made special relativity matter. They would probably die of old age while accelerating. You'd need to be able to accelerate a lot faster, which would most likely also require a way to protect the occupants from the G force. All of this is a long shot, but not physically impossible.
    I suppose the point I'm making is that special relativity for travel is great, as it brings hope once you realise FTL is most likely impossible. But, it's so out of our reach to travel even that fast that it might as well be impossible too.

    If the facts don't fit the theory, the theory gets binned.

    Spot on, during my PhD I came up with evidence that a central dogma of the field, that skeletal muscle needs nerves to innervate it during development to survive and develop was wrong. I had a natural mouse mutant with muscles that never saw a nerve and they developed just fine, up until birth. That dogma was to a large extent built by my supervisor. I took my evidence to him and he said 'that's very interesting, we must make some time to think of how to explore this'. Which is what we did.

    That is the mark of a good scientist who practices what he teaches. He taught me to always follow the data.

    It might not seem earthshattering but it stopped people chasing shadows by grinding up motoneuron terminals looking for a muscle growth factor. It was acetylcholine (the transmitter used to activate muscle) all along.

    It also means if you have an accident that cuts the nerve then electrically stimulating the muscles while the nerve regenerates is all that is needed to stop them degenerating too much.

    OK, let's try again.
    Firstly, i appreciate that English is not your first language, and that means it is sometimes difficult to understand some of your sentences, and that is not entirely your fault. To be fair to you, i don't speak any other languages, so i am not faulting you for that at all.
    However, having said that, i still think you have been insulting and confrontational to me in all your previous messages, so if you continue to do so, i will not talk to you, as this is a subject i know a lot about and it's clear that you don't. I'm sorry, but , even taking the language difficulty into account, you clearly don't - other people have mentioned that to you too.
    This last message from you was both more polite, and contained some questions about actual Physics that make sense, so i will be happy to deal with it - provided that you try to take on board what i'm saying. I will do this in two parts, so please bear with me and be patient, as i need to explain the two different meanings of the word "burning", and this means i need to say a bit about Chemistry before i talk about Nuclear Physics.
    So, on the use of the word "burning" :-
    This is used in Nuclear/Astrophysics, but it does NOT mean burning in the everyday sense,and i realize that this may be confusing. The everyday meaning applies to Chemistry and is what we observe in some chemical reactions when energy in the form of heat/light is given out when the reaction is taking place. This is because, in a chemical reaction, bonds are broken, and then new ones are made. Some reactions produce a lot of energy, and so we see light and feel heat being produced, but it isn't always noticeable, it depends on the reaction.
    A very simple example where it is noticeable : Hydrogen reacts with the Oxygen in the air to form water. Energy has to be put in to the system to make the reaction start ( called the Activation Energy ). This breaks the bonds in the Hydrogen molecules H-H, and in the Oxygen molecules O=O. They then reconfigure to form water molecules, which contain two O-H bonds. When these form, a great deal of energy is released, which is what we perceive as light and heat from the reaction.
    To sum up :- breaking chemical bonds absorbs energy, making chemical bonds releases energy.
    There is a vast amount more that could be said about chemical reactions, but that is all we need at the moment.
    The most important point is that all this happens as a result of changes in the arrangement of electrons on the outside of atoms, so is all to do with the Electromagnetic Force, one of the 4 fundamental forces of Physics. Chemical processes do NOT in any way affect the nuclei of the atoms involved. This is because the structure of the nucleus is governed by 2 of the other 3 fundamental forces, namely the Strong Nuclear Force and the Weak Interaction.
    The weak force is responsible for radioactive decay, while the strong force holds the nucleus together.
    By the way, Gravity ( our last fundamental force ) has nothing to do with the structure of atoms - it holds the Universe together,but not atoms!
    The strong force is ENORMOUSLY stronger than the electromagnetic ( E/M for short from now on ) force, so to affect the nuclei of atoms, we need far more extreme conditions than apply to chemical reactions. This is where stars come in.
    Now, this has been a long post, but i needed to explain about "burning" in the sense of Chemistry so that i can then explain separately its different meaning in the context of Nuclear Physics, so please read it, and reply politely, and if/when you do, i will continue by explaining the answers to your questions about stars. They are good questions by the way.
    At the moment, i have to go and make dinner!

    Hello, you're very welcome. I'm glad it was helpful, and i'm always happy to be asked sensible questions, so, in the order you've asked them:
    1) and 2) go together, so i'll deal with them as one question. I can't reproduce it here, but, if you Google Hertsprung-Russell Diagram, or just H-R Diagram, and have a look, you will see how we classify stars. The diagram plots their luminosity ( measured in multiples of the Sun's luminosity,so that is 1 on this scale ) on the vertical axis versus their surface temperature ( measured in degrees Kelvin, the absolute temperature scale ) on the horizontal axis. What you should see is that there is a broad band running from top left to bottom right, and, if your diagram is in colour which would be best, you will see a change from blue to red. That is the so-called Main Sequence, which is the phase of a star's life when it is "burning", in the sense of nuclear fusion, Hydrogen into Helium in its core.
    The other parts of the diagram, namely the Red Giant Branch, the Supergiant Branch, and the White Dwarf Branch are occupied by stars which are at, or near, the ends of their lives, and are evolving/have evolved away from the Main Sequence.
    When they reach this stage, they are fusing Helium into heavier elements at higher and higher temperatures, all the way up to Iron which is the heaviest element that can be made by nuclear fusion. Elements heavier than Iron are made in Supernova explosions of massive stars at the end of their, very short, lives.
    The word Main refers to the fact that most stars ( >90% ) in our galaxy, and other galaxies are on it. The word Sequence is used to showcase the way the properties of stars change as the surface temperature changes.
    3 ) The "leftovers" are the stars of other spectral types. These correspond to surface temperature/visible star colour,and are, for our Galaxy, with the percentage of the total :
    O, blue, >30,000K, 0,0003%
    B, blue-white,10,000-30,000K, 0.13%
    A, white, 7,500-10,000K, 0,6%
    F, yellow-white, 6,000-7,500K, 3%
    G, yellow, 5,200-6,000K,7.6% ( sun-type stars )
    K, orange, 3,700-5,200K, 12.1%
    M,red, 2,400-3,700K, 76.45%
    If you Google "stellar classification" and look at the Wikipedia page, you will see a much fuller version of this table.
    Basically, the hot, luminous, massive stars are rare, though very visible against the background because they are so bright, whereas the vast majority are smaller and less luminous than the Sun,and go unnoticed by us.
    To bring us back to where we started, Proxima Centauri is itself a dim little red dwarf which, in spite of being so close to the Sun, needs a decent telescope in order to see it at all.
    I hope that all helps - regards.

    Yup, now we have cracked the computation required to make an array of telescopes act like one big telescope here in earth we can do the same in space. Fly an array of cheap (relative to Hubble or the James Webb) telescopes with quite large distances between them and you have a telescope with a huge diameter without having to grind a lens or mirror that big.

    With a big enough telescope like that we can image alien worlds. Up until the recent flyby the best image we had of Pluto was all of 4 pixels in size. With a space array telescope we can do much better than that.

    Note that the ESA is testing the technology to get spacecraft to fly in exquisitely stable spacing to make an orbiting gravity wave detector so the ability to fly an array telescope is here.

    Voyager 1 has no solar sail or, indeed, any propulsion system beyond some primitive thrusters. Since launch, it has accelerated only during slingshots with planets. The rest of the time, it has decelerated under the sun's gravity. Of course it isn't going anywhere fast.

    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_sail
    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_sail

    See the interstellar flight section.

    A solar sail roughly 50 square kilometres in size will be capable of carrying a probe up to 25% light speed, if you first send it in towards the sun (for maximal solar pressure). Ideally, you'd use a slingshot trajectory around Mercury or perhaps Venus.

    At 25% the speed of light, you travel 4 light years in 16 years.

    Yes, there's the acceleration and deceleration to consider, but both will be negligible compared to the transit time between star systems.

    If you want to get the entire time inside 16 years, you are free to apply the calculations given. Remember that you have to factor in both gravity wells. I'd advise using an ion drive for the journey to the inner planet, as it is very fuel efficient. Dump the drive part-way into the slingshot, unless you think you can carry sufficient fuel to be useful in the outer solar system.

    Once light drops below a certain level, the solar sail becomes deadweight. The momentum of the dust colliding with it will exceed the pressure of the sunlight. That's when you dump the solar sail and, if you have fuel left, restart the ion drive.

    However, that only works if the velocity you can gain from doing that exceeds the velocity you lose by having a larger mass.

    The hybrid solution is for when you can't use a solar sail that's any larger but need a larger probe for the data collection and transmission.

    It does complicate deceleration, though.

    Anyways, we have the technology, it all works, and we have the material science. If NASA had the funding for such a mission, they would be capable of starting immediately on construction, no additional fundamental research is required.

    Er, with respect, you need to learn some basic Astrophysics. Your post is one of the most ill-informed about Physics i've ever read on here, and, believe me, that's saying something! Wherre did you get this bizarre nonsense from?
    Right,just for you,i'll have one more go.
    Very low-mass stars, M dwarfs, live the longest, because although they have less nuclear fuel, their internal temperatures are much lower, and the nuclear burning rate is VERY temperature sensitive - it rises approximately exponentially with temperature. So, high-mass stars burn their fuel very fast indeed, so have vastly shorter lifetimes. This is because the rate at which they burn their nuclear fuel is extremely fast in comparison. This is because of fundamental rules in Quantum/Nuclear Physics.
    The Main Sequence lifetime of a star goes approximately as T~ 1/M^2, where M is the stellar mass. This means, roughly, if you double the mass, the lifetime is 4 times shorter, not longer.
    So, an O-class supergiant with a mass of roughly 40 solar masses has a lifetime of 1-10 million years, a G-dwarf star like the Sun has a lifespan of about 10 billion years, while a 0.01-0.1 solar mass M-dwarf has a lifespan of over 1 trillion years.
    For comparison, the Sun has a central temperature of about 15 million degrees, whereas my example 40 solar mass O-type supergiant has a a central temperature of several billion degrees. So, even though it has much more fuel to burn than the Sun, it burns it so much faster, that its Main Sequence lifetime is enormously shorter. You may think this is counter-intuitive, but it is true.
    However, you don't need to take my word for it. Google Stellar Evolution/Stellar Lifetimes, and you will see that it is exactly as i say. Or read any textbook on basic stellar Astrophysics, with particular reference to the Mass-Luminosity Law.
    As for the role of Gravity, it brings interstellar material together to form stars, but the properties of the stars formed depend ENTIRELY on their masses and the chemical composition of the material from which they formed.
    Your post appears to be comparing stars to people - there is no comparison whatsoever.

Newton came up with a theory and people were able to use it to work out precisely what would happen under a wide range of circumstances. They then tested it out and guess what? What the real world did was what the theory predicted it would do. It was a good theory. Then someone noticed that there were a few situations where the theory wasn't completely accurately predicting things. Einstein came up with a more subtle theory, which accurately predicted the discrepancies. Hence it was accepted.

    If you think that science is built on guesswork and edifices of pure logic, no wonder you're confused. That's not how it works at all - it's the complete opposite.

    Science is built on observed facts from the world. As it progresses, it gets better and better and explaining what we see and what we measure, and in greater and greater detail. If the facts don't fit the theory, the theory gets binned.

    An Astrophysics graduate writes:-
    Just to redress the balance slightly, regarding the standard of comments on this article, which are mostly at the completely - ignorant - of - Physics end of the knowledge spectrum, here goes:
    Proxima Centauri is a Red Dwarf Star of spectral class M,which have a surface temperature of approximately 3200K, which is why they appear red. They are by far the most numerous stellar type in the Galaxy,making up approximately 76% of all stars on the Main Sequence, which means stars in the "normal" Hydrogen - burning phase of their lives. By contrast, sunlike stars,of spectral class G, with surface temperatures of approximately 5800K, which consequently appear to be yellow, make up about 7.5% of the Main Sequence. this means that if we take a figure of 100 billion stars in our Galaxy just for simplicity, 76 billion of them would red dwarfs, and 7.5 billion of them would be yellow dwarfs. Thus, there are vastly more candidate stars that may possess Earth - type planets in the red dwarf category. This means that the total amount of Habitable Zone ( hereafter HZ )potentially available is very large, even though it is quite small for an individual red dwarf.
    Next,there is the stellar lifetime to consider. Yellow dwarfs live for about 10 billion years, whereas red dwarfs live for about 1 trillion years, as they burn their nuclear fuel far more slowly, for reasons which are fundamental to nuclear physics. This means that they live extraordinarily long lives compared to the Sun. So, if there any earth like planets there, they will have an enormously long time for life to potentially develop.
    It is true that very many red dwarfs produce intense stellar flares, but it is believed that they only do this early in their lifetimes - the first couple of billion years or so, after which, it is thought that they settle down. Also, toward the end of their lives, they are predicted to evolve not into Red Giants, but into Blue Dwarfs, becoming hotter and more luminous, thus expanding the HZ, but not much larger. This stage is predicted to last for 5-10 billion years, which would be plenty of time for life to potentially develop on any earth type planets present.
    On Tidal Locking:- the comments about atmospheres are woefully misinformed, and i do not intend to write an entire thesis on this subject for obvious reasons of both space and attention span. Google it and find out.
    Suffice it to say that there is no reason why earth type planets could not have thick enough atmospheres to be habitable, even if they are tidally locked. The physicist Charles Adler coined what he called the Anna Karenina Principle*, in which he states:
    All stars are fundamentally the same; all planets are different from one another.
    *Based on the quote All happy families are fundamentally the same; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.
    The properties of any star are fundamentally determined by their mass and chemical composition when they form. ( Called the Vogt - Russell Theorem ) There is relatively little difference in their chemical compositions, since the Universe is mostly Hydrogen and Helium. so their masses determine their luminosities, surface temperatures and lifetimes.
    Planets, on the other hand, are a chaotic mess, and so,with so many possibilities and so many planets out there, there are even likely to be some tidally-locked earth like exoplanets with conditions that could allow the development of some sort of life, not of course that it need be anything like us.
    Finally, i should mention the intermediate category of star, namely the Orange Dwarfs. of spectral class K with surface temperatures of about 4500K. they constitute about 12% of the Main Sequence, have a larger HZ than the red dwarfs, are more stable as far as flares are concerned,and live for up to 100 billion years, so are likely to be better candidates for earth type planets that could support life.

    Proxima Centauri is (roughly) 250,000 times as distance from Earth as Jupiter (which is an average of 5 AU away, give or take).

    Signal strength decreases as the square of distance.

    So to have the same signal strength on Earth as the Galileo probe, you'd need a transmitter about 62 billion times as powerful.

    That's about 36 terawatts. Which is roughly three times humanity's entire power usage for 2013.

    The numbers are obviously rough as hell, but the ballpark is correct.

    That's because you don't understand evolution, 150,000 years isn't that long in evolutionary terms. Whether deaths in pregnancy as a result of a narrow birth canal exerts significant evolutionary pressure depends on a whole load of factors, including how significant is that single factor among all the other causes of deaths in pregnancy. Hypertension, Eclampsia, Haemorrhage, Puerperal fever. Pregnant women die of a host of things, there's little selective pressure for that single trait. Additionally while the mother may die, at that stage, the child may not. Which means that the impact of that single trait is diluted in terms of adverse effects on reproduction.

    Then there is the cost of a wider birth canal, how does it impact on gait, energy costs etc. However what we can say is that there's been a significant adaptive change as a result of the narrow birth canal in human females. Childhood, the extended developmental period after birth would appear to be a result of the amount of neural development that takes place after birth. Humans are significantly more dependent in the years after birth than other primates. That's where the adaptation for a large brain and a small pelvis appears to have exerted it selective effect.

    Every time a new planet is discovered out there journalists make the same question to the baffled astronomers: "is it like Earth?" And the poor scientists look at themselves slightly embarrased and answer "Yeah, well... according to the data we have, yes, it is quite similar to Earth". Given that the only data they have about these planet is a gross estimation of its size and distance to its parent star, that's only saying it's not like Jupiter. Before they can add any nuances to this answer it comes the next lame question, as predictable as the first: "can it harbour life?" And then again, the scientist look at themselves and answer "Yeah, why not?" (It could harbour a Starbucks Coffee Shop, for all that we know about it).
    The planets are deemed "habitable" if it can sustains liquid water on its surface. The problem is, we can't know that just by the distance to its star. There is not liquid water in Venus, which is as similar to Earth as a planet can be, and there's liquid water in Europe - below an ice crust - which far, far away from the so-called Goldilocks Zone of the Sun. We just don't know enough of these planets to say if they resemble Earth or not. It's just pure speculation.
    And know, let's go with some speculation of my own: if it's tidally locked, even if it has a ferromagnetic inner core, it is surely spinning at the same pace as its surface. So, no magnetic field. Then, even if the solar flares hadn't blown up its atmosphere eons ago the radiation would had splat the water molecules of its high atmosphere, and it has not mass enough to retain the hydrogen.
    This is not an Earth-twin; it's our beloved sister's twin, a Venus twin.

    Good idea in principle but we still need some technological development before we can make it work.

There are in the visible universe something like 10 to the 11th power number of galaxies, and each galaxy has something like 10 to the 11th power number of stars, so that is about 10 to the 22nd power of stars, and presumably that or a higher number of planets. Doesn't mean any of them but one have life of any form, but consider this: If we're it, it's pretty strange. Why should life have happened only once in 10^22 chances? It now seems less likely that terrestrial life is unique in the universe. Doesn't mean our lifetimes overlap, or that we'll ever know of each other, but the probability of other life now seems greater than that we're unique.

    We only have an n=1 example of life starting and surviving. There is a finite chance that life on Mars or one of the Saturnian or Jovian icy moons with oceans under the ice could be due to transfer via meteorites. The chance is vanishingly low but not impossible.

    A certified 2nd genesis of life would answer a lot of questions like:
    1. is the subset of amino acids we use to build proteins usual.
    2. Like Earth life does it only use left handed molecules.
    3. Does it use DNA and RNA, if so what is its genetic code (is it a triplet code like in us, which combinations code for which amino acids).
    4. What else is it made of?

    There are more but that is quiet enough to be going on with and can be asked with just simple bacterial type life. If life is more complex we can ask questions about sexual reproduction, modes of development. Lots of stuff.

    4

    At 4.2 light years, the SKA telescope will (once completed) be able to give a radio-spectrum image of the planet that is 32x32 pixels in size. That may not sound much, but it's enough to tell you the basic composition of the atmosphere, the weather patterns (as of 4.2 years ago) and the general climatic conditions.

    We know (thanks to James Lovelock) that we can determine if some form of life exists there, because it will result in two chemicals which are unstable in each other's presence being held in dynamic equilibrium. This is true of any planet with any life on it, whether we understand the chemistry of that life or not. it is something that will always hold true because it's implied by the laws that govern chemistry in general.

    So, for example, Earth's oxygen levels haven't changed significantly over the past 500 million years. Free oxygen is not compatible with methane, so you shouldn't get both coexisting, especially in an electrically active atmosphere with a geologically active planet below. Too much energy. Actually, you should have no free oxygen at all, and there wasn't any for the 4 billion years prior to that.

    Life existed before that 500 million year mark, and the atmosphere was in a different "impossible" dynamic equilibrium then, so it would have been detectable. Because life is a function of the chemical energy involved, anyone observing Earth then and now would know life now was much more complex than life then.

    Knowing the weather and climate yields other information. Weather is shaped by life. That's why destruction of environments on Earth changes where the weather goes. It's very simple. Anyways, knowing the distribution of unstable molecules and knowing the distribution of water molecules (water is incredibly stable, and an incredible solvent, so even if it's not utilized by some living organism, the two will interact - that's a given) will tell you how any life is distributed and how severe the conditions are that it must endure.

    The spectral absorption patterns (which are how you find out what's there and what's where) will also tell you a lot about the ratio of different surface types since they will exclude different frequencies in what they reflect. You won't necessarily be able to identify what the surface is, you only know what it is comprised of. So you'll know what elements are where and - for molecules with absorption lines within the band of frequencies that can both pass through the Proxima b atmosphere and ours, and which are within the band that SKA can detect - what compounds are present. That tells you a lot but not everything. You should be able to determine if life uses carbon or silicon, whether it utilizes water or avoids it, but it would be extremely difficult to determine the mechanisms involved beyond maybe being able to make an educated guess as to whether it uses any of the amino acids that either exist naturally on Earth or have been synthesized.

    All that without ever going there.

    That's more than enough to answer the question of life there. SKA will be able to detect aircraft radar a thousand light years away, so it should have little difficulty with detecting any artificial radio sources from such a short distance. (Inverse square law. As you halve the distance, you quadruple the sensitivity.)

    My guess is that they'll find a dead planet, but I'm also going to guess that the atmosphere (if there is one) and the planet's surface will hold a great many chemical surprises that will greatly improve our understanding of planetary formation. A planet that large can only have an inactive core if it is extremely ancient, so we'll either learn more about the makeup of early Third Generation stars or we'll learn more about the internal chemistry of high-gravity rocky planets.

    4. 2 ly is ~4x10^16 m. The maximum Solar Proble Plus "slingshot" speed is calculated to be ~2x10^5 m/s (0.00066c)

    Assuming that you don't need to accelerate or decelerate, then you're travelling from Earth to Proxima in 4x10^16/2x10^5 s: 2x10^11 s -> 6342 years.

    Still very long either way.

    "What's an 'observable universe'?"

    It's similar to the way in which you can only see a limited part of the Earth...to the horizon...when you are on the sea. So even though all we can see in the universe is huge, we can only see a small part of a much larger universe because most of it is 'over the horizon' so to speak. We can only see that part of the total universe whose light has had time to reach us since the big bang.....what is known as 'the observable universe'.

    To put that incredible figure into perspective - going this fast would get you from the Earth to the Moon in about 1/2 an hour. It is also about 0.067% the speed of light.
    So, to travel 4.2 light years, it would take 0.067 x 720 000 x 60 x 60 x 24 x 365 x 4.2 days

    I can certainly understand the mathematical implications of its size. The problem with you logic is in this paragraph:

    Probability clearly states that there is life beyond ours in the universe due to its size. However, probability also states that because of that extreme size the chance of encountering such life is almost nil.

    You are dealing with a probability that carries huge uncertainty. Because of our very limited evidence base, we really don't know yet what the probability is of life (of any complexity) occurring in any given circumstances. You cannot therefore assume that the frequency with which life will be found across the universe will be so low that we will almost certainly never encounter it - any more than someone can say that it is inevitable, or 50:50. We just don't know - so therefore shouldn't assume that it is a fruitless search.

    Intelligent life is perhaps trickier because of the Fermi paradox someone else described above. However, we are again dealing with a whole range of parameters that carry huge uncertainty, so it is similarly incorrect to draw such a firm conclusion.

    Who do you think gets this grant money? Not the researchers; they're paid a salary to do stuff like teaching.

    I got many thousands in grants over many years, but who benefited? Not my bank account. The money was used entirely to employ young research assistants. It is part of their training. From among them come the next, or next but one, generation of scientific leaders. In fact the money wasn't ever paid to me at all; it went to my university which managed the accounting and the human resources and the employment law, and all that stuff.

    In experimental and observational sciences a lot of the money goes to the payment of highly skilled technicians. In this way the country keeps its highest-level skill base working and alive. The rest usually goes on the purchase of equipment, often equipment that doesn't actually exist and needs to be designed and made specially by companies that you've never heard of but which are a vital part of the "knowledge economy".

    If I wanted a new camera for use on a telescope trying to directly image exo-planets, my first stop would probably be a British company called e2v (which, I presume stands for 'electrons to volts'). They make most of the very large, very sensitive, digital camera sensors used in the world today.

    If I wanted really heavy engineering of extraordinary precision, I'd check out some of the French, Dutch, Italian and German companies that have been involved in the building of the enormous telescopes of the European Southern Observatory. It's their employees, all the way down to the typists and the cleaners, who end up with the grant money in their pockets.

    What a stupid person you are.

    Given that nobody has the faintest idea how probable life is even under the perfect conditions, nobody actually knows whether even the entire range of planets in the observable universe is enough to guarantee there being other life within it. If, for example, the chances of life are so low that there's only one life-bearing planet in a region a thousand times the size of the observable universe, then adding a few extra 'Earth like' planets here and there makes bugger all difference.

    And to all those who argue ' but there must surely be other life out there....given so many planets', it is an irrelevant argument. What actually matters is not how many planets there are...however huge....but the chances of life, which may be smaller in size than the number of planets is huge. You cannot argue 'must' on a sample of one.

    "Billions of planets billions of years older than us but no Faster than light travel because no one has visited us. So either life is rare or more likely FTL travel is impossible"

    You don't need FTL travel. Special relativity. If you were in a ship travelling pretty close to the speed of light, to observers on earth your time will slow down. But to you, space in your direction of motion contracts. You have a shorter distance to travel. You could travel to a star 100 light years away in what seems to you like months, weeks even days, depending on how close to the speed of light you get. Problem is, when you get there and look back at our sun, you will see the light that left at least 100 years earlier. No going back to what you knew when you left.

    Question is, why would anyone, human or alien make such a journey. Only one reason I can think of, colonisation.

    One more problem, the space between the stars might look empty but it is not. Leaving the heliosphere would be like leaving a harbour into a raging storm. You would need some heavy duty shielding to survive that.

    So if we see a bunch of ships heading towards us, we are in trouble.

    24 Aug 2016 18.51

    We know that life requires some sort of solvent (no solvent, no chemistry), and that water is one of the few solvents that remains stable and relatively inert over a wide range of temperatures, and has chemical properties that make it easy for certain kinds of biopolymer to close up naturally into little pockets where out-of-equilibrium chemistry (which, at base, is what life is) can safely happen.

    We know that life requires a chemical energy gradient (basically, a surplus of high-powered electrons in the system to run the out-of-equilibrium chemistry with), and that few things supply such a gradient as well as Oxygen - indeed, that's why Oxygen is toxic to life forms on Earth, let alone anywhere else - a significant chunk of your body chemistry is taken up with dealing with that fact.

    This stuff may bore you, but please try not to insult the people who it doesn't bore - they've given their lives to this stuff. Can you imagine how much you'd know if you'd given your life to knowing it?

    And yet, because it sounds vaguely implausible to your untutored mind, you've come up with a few pub-chat objections, and then had the gall to accuse them of idle guessing.

    It's the Fermi Paradox. The universe is 14 billion years old. There are billions of stars that are billions of years older then ours thus there are billions of planets that could support life.
    If life is very very rare then the size of the universe dictates that the chances of two intelligent species running across each other are minuscule.
    If life is common then one of those billions of planets would have given rise to life already and it would have had billions of years to develop space travel were that possible. Since we have never been visited by aliens with space travel the implication is that either life is very very rare or space travel (FTL) is impossible. In either of these circumstances we will never meet intelligent alien life.
    That's roughly it

    While it may please you to come over all high-handed with the little people, you have literally no rigorous basis on which to make that claim. We haven't the first clue how likely life is. It could well be in nearby star systems where we can at least observe its broad chemical processes via spectroscopy and the like. It can't even be ruled out in other places in our own solar system (the more we know about it the more likely Europa looks, for example).

    We will almost certainly never journey to other planets or talk to aliens, but it's entirely feasible given the ongoing development of imaging technology that we may one day satisfy ourselves that there's some sort of biology going on on other worlds.

    “Look again at that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us. On it everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives. The aggregate of our joy and suffering, thousands of confident religions, ideologies, and economic doctrines, every hunter and forager, every hero and coward, every creator and destroyer of civilization, every king and peasant, every young couple in love, every mother and father, hopeful child, inventor and explorer, every teacher of morals, every corrupt politician, every "superstar," every "supreme leader," every saint and sinner in the history of our species lived there-on a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam.

    The Earth is a very small stage in a vast cosmic arena. Think of the endless cruelties visited by the inhabitants of one corner of this pixel on the scarcely distinguishable inhabitants of some other corner, how frequent their misunderstandings, how eager they are to kill one another, how fervent their hatreds. Think of the rivers of blood spilled by all those generals and emperors so that, in glory and triumph, they could become the momentary masters of a fraction of a dot.

    Our posturings, our imagined self-importance, the delusion that we have some privileged position in the Universe, are challenged by this point of pale light. Our planet is a lonely speck in the great enveloping cosmic dark. In our obscurity, in all this vastness, there is no hint that help will come from elsewhere to save us from ourselves.

    The Earth is the only world known so far to harbor life. There is nowhere else, at least in the near future, to which our species could migrate. Visit, yes. Settle, not yet. Like it or not, for the moment the Earth is where we make our stand.

    It has been said that astronomy is a humbling and character-building experience. There is perhaps no better demonstration of the folly of human conceits than this distant image of our tiny world. To me, it underscores our responsibility to deal more kindly with one another, and to preserve and cherish the pale blue dot, the only home we've ever known.”

    ― Carl Sagan, Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space
